## Overview

### Background and Motivation

Urban mobility refers to the movement of people and goods across all transport modes within and between cities. With population growth and climate pressures, Cities are developing smart and sustainable transport systems to enhance accessibility and reduce carbon emissions.

During the progress, massive amounts of data are generated from technologies that track people using public transport such as buses, MRT, and roads from smart cards, GPS, and RFID systems. For instance, tap-on and tap-off data from smart cards capture trip flows from origins to destinations, and discounts are often offered for off-peak travel at the tap-off point.

Yet, such data are often used only for simple GIS mapping, rather than for deeper spatial analyses that could reveal richer insights into mobility patterns.

### Methods & Objective

Using **Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA)** and **Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)** , this exercise aims to analyse bus trips generated by origin at the hexagon level during **three** peak periods:

-   weekday morning (6 am – 9 am),

-   weekday afternoon (5 pm – 8 pm),

-   weekend/holiday (11 am – 8 pm).

Through the progress, our goals are to identify specific locations where values are significantly clustered or dispersed, and to reveal how hot and cold spots evolve over time. We hope to discover emerging travel trends for more responsive transport planning.

### Importing the Geospatial Ploygon Data: Master Plan 2019 Subzone

The code chunk below imports Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) from Singapore’s open data portal.

```{r}
mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml")
```

```{r}
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  # return NA if missing or empty
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)          #parse the HTML string 
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")  #get all table rows <tr>
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>% #keep row where <th> table header text = field_name
    html_element("td") %>%                                       #take its <td> table data
    html_text2()                                                 #extract clean text
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value        #return NA if no match, otherwise the value
}
```

```{r}
mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(
     #for each description string, call the function, It returns a length-1 character per row (or NA)
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>% #drop the raw KML attributes
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col()) #move the geometry column to the end
```

```{r}
class(mpsz)
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
st_crs(mpsz)
```

Since there are a few points located outside the Singapore boundary, these need to be excluded. If we encounter an error message such as st_crs(x) != st_crs(y), it indicates that the coordinate reference systems (CRS) of the two objects are not the same. In such cases, we should assign the correct and consistent CRS (i.e., EPSG:3414). Both st_transform() and st_set_crs() can be used to apply the appropriate CRS.

### Creating the analytical hexagons (Singapore with Honeycomb Grid)

-   cellsize: A numeric value (length 1 or 2) specifying the target cell size. For square/rectangular cells, this defines width and height. For hexagonal cells, it defines the distance between opposite edges. So for the actual analysis, we should use `cellsize = 750`.

```{r}
hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz,
                        cellsize = 750,  ## attention 375m required for take-home ex.
                        what = "polygon",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()                                ## this st_* function doesn't return sf data.frame, we need to specifically coerce the file to sf object.

```

## Selecting hexagons with bus stops

### Filtering hexagons with bus stops

To implement this, we first filter the hexagons using a spatial intersection with the bus-stop points.

Recall: st_intersection() returns the geometric overlap (catchment), while st_intersects() returns a logical relation (TRUE/FALSE). After filtering, the hexagon count is reduced from 4,524 to 924.

```{r}
hexagon$busstop_count = 
  lengths(st_intersects(hexagon, BusStop_in_SG))
```

```{r}
hexagon <- filter(hexagon, busstop_count >0)
```

## Preparing Trip Generation Data

### Cleaning the data

Year_Month and destination_pt_code can be excluded from this analysis.

```{r}
# select the variables
trips <- odbus %>%
  select (c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>%
  rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>%  # easier when performing join later
  rename(HOUR_OF_DAY= TIME_PER_HOUR) %>%
  rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS) #easy interpretation
```

The BUS_STOP_N (post code of bus stop origination) is converted to factor since they are unique identifier and easier grouping group_by later.

```{r}
trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N)
kable(head(trips))
```

### Populating Hexagon IDs into BusStop data frame

Next, we combine the hexagon, bus stop, and trip datasets.

This code creates a lookup table linking each bus stop BUS_STOP_N to the hexagon it belongs to HEX_ID.

```{r}
bs_hex <- st_intersection(
  BusStop, hexagon) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID))

kable(head(bs_hex))
```

```{r}
write_rds(bs_hex, "data/rds/bs_hex.rds")
```

### Adding HEX_ID into bus trips data

The code chunk below merges the HEX_ID and Bus Stop into trip.

```{r}
trips<- inner_join(trips, bs_hex)
kable(head(trips))
```

### Aggregating TRIPS based on HEX_ID

The code chunk below groups trip volume by **HEX_ID, DATE_TYPE, and HOUR_OF_DAY**.

```{r}
trips_wide <- trips%>%
  group_by(
    HEX_ID,
    DAY_TYPE,
    HOUR_OF_DAY) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = HOUR_OF_DAY,
              values_from = TRIPS)

trips_wide[is.na(trips_wide)] <- 0
  
colnames(trips_wide)
```

### Filter Peak Periods

The code chunk below adds up the trip volume per Hexagon for **three** peak periods and creates three new columns:

-   weekday morning (6 am – 9 am) as "WEEKDAY_AM"

-   weekday afternoon (5 pm – 8 pm) as "WEEKDAY_PM"

-   weekend/holiday (11 am – 8 pm) as "WEEKEND"

```{r}
peak_trips <- trips_wide %>%
  mutate(
    WEEKDAY_AM = if_else(
      DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY",
      rowSums(.[3:5], na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_
    ),
    WEEKDAY_PM = if_else(
      DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY",
      rowSums(.[14:16], na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_
    ),
    WEEKEND = if_else(
      DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY",
      rowSums(.[8:16], na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_)) %>%
  select(HEX_ID, WEEKDAY_AM, WEEKDAY_PM, WEEKEND) %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(
    WEEKDAY_AM = sum(WEEKDAY_AM, na.rm = TRUE),
    WEEKDAY_PM = sum(WEEKDAY_PM, na.rm = TRUE),
    WEEKEND = sum(WEEKEND, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
 
```

We have a quick overview on the newly creately `peak_trips` data.

```{r}
kable(head(peak_trips, 10))
```

In total, the number of hex cells was reduced from 924 to 824.

for example, since bus stops 0000 (Changi Airport) and 00000 (Changi Bay) from the Bus Stop Locations dataset have no passenger tap-on data, the corresponding hex cell HEX_ID 834 was excluded after the join.

Similarly, bus stop 31029 (Western Water Catchment, no man's land) and its corresponding hex cell HEX_ID 082 were excluded.



### Create Space-time Cube for EHSA

EHSA requires multiple time steps to detect trends. Here we prepare the data for each peak period.

```{r}
trips_long <- trips_wide%>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(3:26),
    names_to = "HOUR_OF_DAY",
    values_to = "TRIPS")
```

```{r}
peak_hours <- trips_long%>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY" & HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6,7,8,17,18,19) | 
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY"& HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19)) %>%
  mutate(HOUR_OF_DAY = as.numeric(HOUR_OF_DAY), HEX_ID = as.character(HEX_ID))
```

We have a quick overview on the newly creately `peak_hours` data.

```{r}
kable(head(peak_hours, 10))
```

```{r}
peak_hours_hex <-left_join(peak_hours, hexagon) %>%
  st_as_sf()
```

There are two ways to create spacetime objects using `as_spacetime()` or `spacetime()`. The first method transforms `sf` object that contains location IDs, time and geometry into a spacetime object.The second way create a space object from two separate objects one for geometry and another one for attribute data.

The code chunk below uses the former approach with [`as_spacetime()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/as_spacetime) of **sfdep** to create an [**spatio-temporal cube**](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/articles/spacetime-s3.html) and verifies the class using `is_spacetime_cube()`.

```{r}
# 1. Weekday Morning Peak (6-9am)
peak_am <- peak_hours_hex %>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6,7,8)) %>%
  select(1,4,5,3) %>%
  arrange(HOUR_OF_DAY)
am_st <- as_spacetime(peak_am,.loc_col = "HEX_ID", .time_col ="HOUR_OF_DAY")
is_spacetime_cube(am_st)

```

```{r}
# 2. Weekday Afternoon Peak (5-8pm)  
peak_pm <- peak_hours_hex %>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17,18,19))%>%
  select(1,4,5,3)%>%
  arrange(HOUR_OF_DAY)

pm_st <- as_spacetime(peak_pm,.loc_col = "HEX_ID", .time_col ="HOUR_OF_DAY")
is_spacetime_cube(pm_st)
```

```{r}
# 3. Weekend/Holiday Peak (11am-8pm)
peak_weekend <- peak_hours_hex %>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY", HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19))%>%
  select(1,4,5,3)%>%
  arrange(HOUR_OF_DAY)
weekend_st <- as_spacetime(peak_weekend,.loc_col = "HEX_ID", .time_col ="HOUR_OF_DAY")
is_spacetime_cube(weekend_st)
```

```{r}
mpsz_pop25 <- mpsz_pop25 %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = ifelse(is.na(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`), 0, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`))%>%
  mutate(`EAR` = ifelse(is.na(`TOTAL`), 0, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`/ `TOTAL` ))%>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY = ifelse(is.na(DEPENDENCY), 0, DEPENDENCY)) %>%
  mutate(EAR = ifelse(is.na(EAR), 0, EAR))
```

```{r}
hex_pop <- st_intersection(hexagon, mpsz_pop25) %>%
  mutate(overlap_area = st_area(.)) %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(DEPENDENCY = weighted.mean(DEPENDENCY, as.numeric(overlap_area), na.rm = TRUE),
           EAR = weighted.mean(EAR, as.numeric(overlap_area), na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = 'drop')
```

```{r}
peak_hex_pop <-left_join(peak_trips, hex_pop)
```

```{r}
peak_hex_with_subzone <- peak_hex %>%
  st_intersection(mpsz %>% select(SUBZONE_N)) %>%
  mutate(overlap_area = st_area(.)) %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  arrange(desc(overlap_area)) %>%
  slice(1) %>%  # Keep the subzone with largest overlap
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-overlap_area)
```

```{r}
write_rds(peak_hex_with_subzone, "data/rds/peak_hex_with_subzone.rds")
```

### Creating Space-time Cube

```{r}
st_cube <- peak_hex %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(WEEKDAY_AM, WEEKDAY_PM, WEEKEND),
    names_to = "PERIOD",
    values_to = "TRIPS"
  ) %>%
  mutate(TIME_INDEX = case_when(
    PERIOD == "WEEKDAY_AM" ~ 1,
    PERIOD == "WEEKDAY_PM" ~ 2, 
    PERIOD == "WEEKEND" ~ 3
  ))
```

```{r}
locations <- st_cube %>%
    distinct(HEX_ID, geometry)

st_peak <- spacetime(st_cube, locations,
                    .loc_col = "HEX_ID", 
                    .time_col = "TIME_INDEX")

```

```{r}
write_rds(st_peak, "data/rds/st_peak.rds")
```

```{r}
st_peak <- read_rds("data/rds/st_peak.rds")
```

## EDA

### Percentile Map

The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0-1%,1-10%, 10-50%,50-90%,90-99%, and 99-100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be derived by means of the base R quantile command, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1). Note that the begin and endpoint need to be included.

The code chunk checks that there are no missing trip records in all 3 peak periods for each hexagon.

```{r}
peak_hex <- peak_hex %>%
  drop_na()
```

```{r}
sum(is.na(peak_hex[["WEEKDAY_AM"]]))
sum(is.na(peak_hex[["WEEKDAY_PM"]]))
sum(is.na(peak_hex[["WEEKEND"]]))
```

The code chunk below creates functions to plot a percentile map for selected variable in the data frame.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View code"
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% 
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map", filename = "animated.gif") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  var <- as.vector(unlist(var))
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Create the animated map
  tm_shape(mpsz) +
    tm_fill("gray",fill_alpha =0.5) +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            fill.scale = tm_scale(
              breaks = bperc,
              values = "-RdBu",         
              value.na = NA,            
              labels = c("<1%", "1–10%", "10–50%", "50–90%", "90–99%", ">99%")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(
              title = legtitle,
              na.show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle)+
    tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
    tm_scale_bar() +
    tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
    tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall",
            position = c("right", "bottom"))
}
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View code"
boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}


get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  var <- as.vector(unlist(var))
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_fill("gray",fill_alpha =0.5) +
  tm_shape(df) +
        tm_fill(vnam,
        fill.scale = tm_scale(
        breaks = bb,
        values = "-RdBu",         
        value.na = NA,            
        labels = c("lower outlier", 
                     "< 25%", 
                     "25% - 50%", 
                     "50% - 75%",
                     "> 75%", 
                     "upper outlier")),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = legtitle,        
        na.show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle) +
    tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
    tm_scale_bar() +
    tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
    tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall",
            position = c("right", "bottom"))
}
```

```{r}
get.var <- function(vname, df) {

    st_set_geometry(NULL)

percentmap_animated <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map", filename = "animated.gif") {
  # Calculate percentile breaks using the parameters
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)  # Use vnam parameter
  var <- as.vector(unlist(var))
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent, na.rm = TRUE)

  animated_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
    tm_fill("gray", fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_shape(df) +  
    tm_fill(vnam,   
            fill.scale = tm_scale(
              breaks = bperc,
              values = "-RdBu",         
              value.na = NA,
              labels = c("<1%", "1–10%", "10–50%", "50–90%", "90–99%", ">99%")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(
              title = legtitle,
              na.show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
    tm_scalebar() +
    tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
    tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall",
              position = c("right", "bottom")) +
    tm_animate(frames = "HOUR_OF_DAY", fps = 1, play = "loop") +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle)  
  
  full_path <- file.path("img", filename)  
  # Create the animation
  tmap_animation(animated_map,
                 filename = full_path,
                 width = 1000, 
                 height = 600)
}
```

## GMSA

Global Measures of Spatial Association

Intro

The contiguity based spatial weights are generated with row standardisation, where each neighbor contributes equally and the weights for each polygon sum to 1. Despite 3 isolated hexagons (0.36% of observations), this approach will be used for consistency. The amount of isolated units does not substantially affect inference, and most areas exhibit the expected 6 neighbours as under analytical hexagon structure.

### Weekday Morning Peak

#### Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights: sfdep method

```{r}
wm_q_wam <- weekday_am %>%
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry, queen = TRUE), #queen is default method in st_contiguity
         wt = st_weights(
           nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE), # allow_zero is enabled to capture the zero
         .before = 1)
summary(wm_q_wam$nb)
```

```{r}
wm_k_wam <- weekday_am %>%
  mutate(nb = st_knn(geometry, k = 6), #queen is default method in st_contiguity
         wt = st_weights(
           nb, style = "W"), # allow_zero is enabled to capture the zero
         .before = 1)
summary(wm_k_wam$nb)
```

#### Computing Global Moran's I

In the code chunk below, [`global_moran()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/global_moran) function is used to compute the Moran’s I value. Different from spdep package, the output is a tibble data.frame.

```{r}
moranI_wam_q <- global_moran(wm_q_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                       wm_q_wam$nb,
                       wm_q_wam$wt, zero.policy = TRUE)
glimpse(moranI_wam_q)
```

```{r}
moranI_wam_k <- global_moran(wm_k_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                       wm_k_wam$nb,
                       wm_k_wam$wt)
glimpse(moranI_wam_k)
```

#### Performing Global Moran’s I test

Moran’s I test can be performed by using [`global_moran_test()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/global_moran_test.html) as shown in the code chunk below.

```{r}
global_moran_test(wm_q_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                       wm_q_wam$nb,
                       wm_q_wam$wt, zero.policy = TRUE)
```

The default for `alternative` argument is *“two.sided”*. Other supported arguments are “greater” or “less”. By default the `randomization` argument is *TRUE*. If FALSE, under the assumption of normality.

```{r}
global_moran_test(wm_k_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                       wm_k_wam$nb,
                       wm_k_wam$wt)
```

#### Performing Global Moran’I permutation test

[`global_moran_perm()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/global_moran_perm.html) is used to perform 100 Monte Carlo simulations.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
```

```{r}
wamiperm <- global_moran_perm(wm_q_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                  wm_q_wam$nb,
                  wm_q_wam$wt,
                  nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE) #100 simulations since the it starts with 0.

wamiperm
summary(wamiperm[["res"]])
```

The code chunk below uses hist() and abline() of R Graphic to visualise the simulated Moran’s I test in detail.

```{r}
hist(wamiperm$res,freq = TRUE, breaks = 20,
     xlab = "Simulated Moran's I")
abline(v = 0, col = "red") # v is to set x value for vertical line
```

**At the 95% confidence level, p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. Moran's I value is 0.3 which is a sign of moderate clustering.**

```{r}
wamkiperm <-global_moran_perm(wm_k_wam$WEEKDAY_AM,
                  wm_k_wam$nb,
                  wm_k_wam$wt,
                  nsim = 99) #100 simulations since the it starts with 0.
wamkiperm
```

```{r}
hist(wamkiperm$res,freq = TRUE, breaks = 20,
     xlab = "Simulated Moran's I")
abline(v = 0, col = "red") # v is to set x value for vertical line
```

## Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA)

They identify specific locations where values are significantly clustered or dispersed. Unlike global measures that summarise the whole map, LMSA tests each location to detect hotspots (high-value clusters), cold spots (low-value clusters), and spatial outliers.

## LISA Map

LISA map is a categorical map showing outliers and clusters throught combining local Moran’s I of geographical areas and their respective p-values.

In this section, we use [`local_moran()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/local_moran.html) of sfdep package to compute Local Moran’s I of Bus Trips at analytical hexagon level.

There are a few columns that will be gereated by `local_moran()`:

-   ii: the local Moran’s I statistics for each region

-   e.ii: expected value of ii under spatial randomness

-   var.ii: the variance of local moran statistic under null model

-   z.ii:the standard deviate of local moran statistic (z-value)

-   p.ii: the p-value of local moran statistic

-   p_ii_sim: p-value from randomisation (Monte Carlo simulations)

-   p_folded_sim: p-value from k-folded simulations (more conservative, treats extreme values both tails), from pysal (python’s equivalent ESDA).

-   skewness, kurtosis: diagnostics for the distribution of simulated ii values (shape compared to normal)

-   mean, median,pysal: mean, median, quandrant classifications based on comparing the region’s value to the value of neighbours, in the format of self - neighbours, e.g., “High-High”.

 There are two types of outliers i.e. High-Low and Low-High outliers and two types of clusters: High-High and Low-Low. 
 
| Type | Description |
|----|----|
| High–High | A hex with high trip values surrounded by other high-value hexes. |
| Low–Low | A hex with low trip values surrounded by other low-value hexes. |
| High–Low | A hex with high trip value but surrounded by low-value neighbours. |
| Low–High | A hex with low trip value but surrounded by high-value neighbours. |

### Weekday Morning Peak

#### Computing local Moran’s I

The code chunk below calculates Local Moran’s I of Bus Trips at analytical hexagon level by using [`local_moran()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/local_moran.html) of sfdep package.

```{r}
lisa_wam_q <- wm_q_wam %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKDAY_AM, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wam_q))
```

The `local_moran()` function returns a matrix of values. We use `unnest()` to expand it into separate columns so they can be accessed directly in the `lisa_x` sf object.


```{r}
#KNN method
lisa_wam_k <- wm_k_wam %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKDAY_AM, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wam_k))
```

#### Visualising Local Moran’s I and p-value of Local Moran's I

In this code chunk below, tmap functions are used prepare two choropleth maps by using value in the ii field and p_ii_sim field side by side.

```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}
tmap_mode("plot")

ii.map_wam_q <-tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_fill("gray", fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(lisa_wam_q) +
  tm_fill("ii",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "pretty",
      n = 5,
      values = "-brewer.RdBu",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local Moran's I",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tm_title("Local Moran's I of Bus Trips \nWeekday Morning Peak (Queen's method)") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall",
             position = c("right", "bottom"))
 
p_ii_sim.map_wam_q <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_fill("gray", fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(lisa_wam_q) +
  tm_fill("p_ii_sim",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
      labels = c("<0.001","0.001-0.01", "0.01-0.05", "Insignificant >0.05"),
      values = "-turbo"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "p-value",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tm_title("p-values of Loal Moran's I of Bus Trips \nWeekday Morning Peak (Queen's method)")+
  tm_options(legend.na.show = FALSE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
```

#### Plotting LISA map

LISA visualisation highlights spatial patterns such as hot spots, cold spots, and outliers using tools like **choropleth maps, Moran scatterplots, and hot spot maps**.

##### Plotting Moran Scatterplot

A Moran Scatterplot visualises spatial autocorrelation by plotting a variable against its spatial lag, with the slope representing Moran’s I and points indicating clusters or outliers.

The code chunk below uses [`st_lag()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/st_lag) of **sfdep** package to calculate the spatial lag variable for `lisa$WEEKDAY_AM`.

```{r}
lisa_wam_q <- lisa_wam_q %>%
  mutate(lag_WEEKDAY_AM = st_lag(
    WEEKDAY_AM, nb, wt, allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1)%>%
  unnest(lag_WEEKDAY_AM)
```

KNN method

```{r}

lisa_wam_k <- lisa_wam_k %>%
  mutate(lag_WEEKDAY_AM = st_lag(
    WEEKDAY_AM, nb, wt, allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1)%>%
  unnest(lag_WEEKDAY_AM)
```

Then code chunk plots the Moran Scatterplot of Trips by using ggplot.

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_q,
       aes(x = WEEKDAY_AM, y = lag_WEEKDAY_AM)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth( method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +   #linear model
  labs (x = "WEEKDAY_AM", Y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
        title = "Morgan Scatterpolot (Queen's method)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_k,
       aes(x = WEEKDAY_AM, y = lag_WEEKDAY_AM)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth( method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +   #linear model
  labs (x = "WEEKDAY_AM", Y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
        title = "Morgan Scatterpolot (KNN method)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The code below updates the scatterplot with colour coding, where top right quadrant, red points represent regions with high values and high neighbourhood averages (**High–High clusters**).

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_q, 
       aes(x = WEEKDAY_AM, 
           y = lag_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", #linear model
              se = FALSE, # hide confidence intervals 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wam_q$lag_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa_wam_q$WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "WEEKDAY_AM",
       y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
       title = "Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants (QUEEN)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_k, 
       aes(x = WEEKDAY_AM, 
           y = lag_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", #linear model
              se = FALSE, # hide confidence intervals 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wam_k$lag_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa_wam_k$WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "WEEKDAY_AM",
       y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
       title = "Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants (KNN)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

##### Plotting Moran Scatterplot with Standardised Variable

The code chunk below uses [`scale()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/scale) to center and scale the GDPPC, centering subtracts the mean (ignoring NAs) from the variables, and scaling divides the result by its standard deviation, converting the values to z-scores.

```{r}
lisa_wam_q <- lisa_wam_q %>%
  mutate(
    z_WEEKDAY_AM = as.vector(scale(WEEKDAY_AM)),
    z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM = as.vector(scale(lag_WEEKDAY_AM)),
    .before = 1)
```

knn

```{r}
lisa_wam_k <- lisa_wam_k %>%
  mutate(
    z_WEEKDAY_AM = as.vector(scale(WEEKDAY_AM)),
    z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM = as.vector(scale(lag_WEEKDAY_AM)),
    .before = 1)
```

The function [`as.vector()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pbdDMAT/versions/0.5-1/topics/as.vector) goes around the `scale()` function, to ensure the output is converted to numeric vector from matrix.

The code chunk below plot the Morgan Scatterplot.

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_q, 
       aes(x = z_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           y = z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wam_q$z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa_wam_q$z_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised WEEKDAY_AM",
       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants (QUEEN)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wam_k, 
       aes(x = z_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           y = z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wam_k$z_lag_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa_wam_k$z_WEEKDAY_AM), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised WEEKDAY_AM",
       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of WEEKDAY_AM",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants (KNN)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

##### Preparing LISA Map Classes

The code chunk below sets a statistical significance level for the local Moran.

```{r}
signif <- 0.05
```

##### Plotting and visualising LISA map

The code chunk below prepares LISA map by deriving a new field called **LISA-cluster** from one of the three LISA classes (**`mean,median, pysal`**). Only significant regions (p \< 0.05) keep their cluster label, others are assigned as "insignificant". Then clusters are ordered by levels.

```{r}
lisa_wam_q <- lisa_wam_q %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse( p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor( LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")))
```

```{r}
lisa_wam_k <- lisa_wam_k %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse( p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor( LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")))
```

The code chunk below visualises the clusters in the LISA map.

```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}

tmap_mode("plot")

lisa_map_wam_q <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_fill("gray", fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(lisa_wam_q) + 
  tm_fill("LISA_cluster",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
      values = c(
        "grey80",      # Insignificant
        "blue",        # Low-Low
        "lightblue",   # Low-High
        "pink",        # High-Low
        "red"          # High-High
      )
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "LISA Cluster",
      position = tm_pos_in("left","bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tm_title("Local Moran's I Clusters (p < 0.05) \nWeekday Morning Peak (Queen's method)") +
  tm_options(legend.na.show = FALSE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall",
             position = c("right", "bottom"))

lisa_map_wam_q
```

### Weekday Afternoon Peak

#### Computing local Moran’s I

The code chunk below calculates Local Moran’s I of Bus Trips at analytical hexagon level by using [`local_moran()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/local_moran.html) of sfdep package.

```{r}
lisa_wpm_q <- wm_q_wpm %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKDAY_PM, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wpm_q))
```

The `local_moran()` function returns a matrix of values. We use `unnest()` to expand it into separate columns so they can be accessed directly in the `lisa_x` sf object.


```{r}
#KNN method
lisa_wpm_k <- wm_k_wpm %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKDAY_PM, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wpm_k))
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wpm_k, 
       aes(x = z_WEEKDAY_PM, 
           y = z_lag_WEEKDAY_PM, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wam_k$z_lag_WEEKDAY_PM), lty=2) +

  theme_minimal()
```

##### Preparing LISA Map Classes

The code chunk below sets a statistical significance level for the local Moran.

```{r}
signif <- 0.05
```

##### Plotting and visualising LISA map

The code chunk below prepares LISA map by deriving a new field called **LISA-cluster** from one of the three LISA classes (**`mean,median, pysal`**). Only significant regions (p \< 0.05) keep their cluster label, others are assigned as "insignificant". Then clusters are ordered by levels.

```{r}
lisa_wpm_q <- lisa_wpm_q %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse( p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor( LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")))
```

```{r}
lisa_wpm_k <- lisa_wpm_k %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse( p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor( LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")))
```

The code chunk below visualises the clusters in the LISA map.

```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}

  tm_shape(lisa_wpm_q) +

        "pink",        # High-Low
        "red"          # High-High
      )

      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tm_title("Local Moran's I Clusters (p < 0.05) \nWeekday Afternoon Peak (Queen's method)") +

  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +

lisa_map_wpm_q
```

### Weekends/Holiday Peak

#### Computing local Moran’s I

The code chunk below calculates Local Moran’s I of Bus Trips at analytical hexagon level by using [`local_moran()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/local_moran.html) of sfdep package.

```{r}
lisa_wkd_q <- wm_q_wkd %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKEND, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wkd_q))
```

The `local_moran()` function returns a matrix of values. We use `unnest()` to expand it into separate columns so they can be accessed directly in the `lisa_x` sf object.


```{r}
#KNN method
lisa_wkd_k <- wm_k_wkd %>% 
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    WEEKEND, nb, wt, nsim = 99, zero.policy = TRUE),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

```{r}
kable(head(lisa_wkd_k))
```

#### Plotting LISA map


LISA visualisation highlights spatial patterns such as hot spots, cold spots, and outliers using tools like **choropleth maps, Moran scatterplots, and hot spot maps**.

##### Plotting Moran Scatterplot

A Moran Scatterplot visualises spatial autocorrelation by plotting a variable against its spatial lag, with the slope representing Moran’s I and points indicating clusters or outliers.

The code chunk below uses [`st_lag()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/st_lag) of **sfdep** package to calculate the spatial lag variable for `lisa$WEEKEND`.

```{r}
lisa_wkd_q <- lisa_wkd_q %>%
  mutate(lag_WEEKEND = st_lag(
    WEEKEND, nb, wt, allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1)%>%
  unnest(lag_WEEKEND)
```

KNN method

```{r}

lisa_wkd_k <- lisa_wkd_k %>%
  mutate(lag_WEEKEND = st_lag(
    WEEKEND, nb, wt, allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1)%>%
  unnest(lag_WEEKEND)
```

Then code chunk plots the Moran Scatterplot of Trips by using ggplot.

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wkd_q,
       aes(x = WEEKEND, y = lag_WEEKEND)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth( method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +   #linear model
  labs (x = "WEEKEND", Y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKEND",
        title = "Morgan Scatterpolot (Queen's method)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

KNN
```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wkd_k,
       aes(x = WEEKEND, y = lag_WEEKEND)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth( method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +   #linear model
  labs (x = "WEEKEND", Y = "Spatial Lag of WEEKEND",
        title = "Morgan Scatterpolot (KNN method)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The code below updates the scatterplot with colour coding, where top right quadrant, red points represent regions with high values and high neighbourhood averages (**High–High clusters**).

```{r}

  theme_minimal()
```

##### Plotting Moran Scatterplot with Standardised Variable

The code chunk below uses [`scale()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/scale) to center and scale the GDPPC, centering subtracts the mean (ignoring NAs) from the variables, and scaling divides the result by its standard deviation, converting the values to z-scores.

```{r}
lisa_wkd_q <- lisa_wkd_q %>%
  mutate(
    z_WEEKEND= as.vector(scale(WEEKEND)),
    z_lag_WEEKEND = as.vector(scale(lag_WEEKEND)),
    .before = 1)
```

knn

```{r}
lisa_wkd_k <- lisa_wkd_k %>%
  mutate(
    z_WEEKEND = as.vector(scale(WEEKEND)),
    z_lag_WEEKEND = as.vector(scale(lag_WEEKEND)),
    .before = 1)
```

The function [`as.vector()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pbdDMAT/versions/0.5-1/topics/as.vector) goes around the `scale()` function, to ensure the output is converted to numeric vector from matrix.

The code chunk below plot the Morgan Scatterplot.

```{r}
ggplot(data = lisa_wkd_q, 
       aes(x = z_WEEKEND, 
           y = z_lag_WEEKEND, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa_wkd_q$z_lag_WEEKEND), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa_wkd_q$z_WEEKEND), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised WEEKEND",
       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of WEEKEND",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants (QUEEN)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Box Map for LISA

Two more steps are required before we begin the analysis:

Convert the data into a space–time cube to run EHSA on that cube.
